name: TPS60151DRVR
title: TPS60151: 5 V, 140 mA regulated charge pump
summary: A switched-capacitor doubler that makes a regulated 5 V from a 2.7 V to 5.5 V input, holding regulation with the input above 5 V too. It delivers at least 140 mA for VIN above 3.3 V, switches at 1.5 MHz and needs only three capacitors. Below about 8 mA of load it skips pulses and draws 90 μA. Current limit, short-circuit foldback, output reverse current blocking, soft start, UVLO and thermal shutdown are built in; it comes in a 2 mm × 2 mm 6-pin WSON.

circuits.title: Typical application schematic
circuits.description: The basic 5 V doubler. C1 holds up the supply at VIN, C3 is the reservoir on the 5 V output and C2 is the pump capacitor between CP- and CP+. ENA is brought out as an enable/disable input.

circuits.title: Application circuit for OTG system
circuits.description: The charge pump makes the 5 V VBUS rail of a battery-powered USB On-The-Go device. The device's own 2.7 V to 5.5 V supply feeds VIN; the 5 V output returns to the device, which holds a controller, a comparator and a USB transceiver, carries the rail to the VBUS pin of the USB socket and drives ENA. C1 decouples VIN, C3 is the output capacitor and C2 the flying capacitor. Available output current is 140 mA with VIN at 3.3 V or more and 50 mA with VIN at 2.7 V or more.

parts.value: OTG device: controller, comparator, USB transceiver
USB socket: VBUS, GND, ID, D+, D-

notes: Output current: 140 mA for VIN ≥ 3.3 V, 50 mA for VIN ≥ 2.7 V.

circuits.title: Application circuit for driving white LEDs
circuits.description: The 5 V output runs five white LEDs in parallel for a small display backlight, each LED in series with its own ballast resistor from VOUT to ground. C1 decouples VIN, C3 is the output capacitor and C2 the flying capacitor; ENA is the enable input.
notes: Output current: 140 mA for VIN ≥ 3.3 V, 50 mA for VIN ≥ 2.7 V.

circuits.title: Output reverse current test setup
circuits.description: Measures the current pushed back into VOUT. A source Vpre_bias holds the output node at a set voltage while VIN is driven, open or shorted and ENA is high or low; the current it delivers into VOUT is Ireverse. C1 is on VIN, C3 on VOUT and C2 between CP- and CP+.

equations.name: Output voltage
equations.expr: Vout = VIN – VQ1 + V(CF) – VQ4 = VIN – VQ1 + 2.5 V – VQ4 = 5 V (ideal)

where.V(CF): voltage held on the flying capacitor, regulated to 2.5 V

equations.name: Flying capacitor charge balance
equations.expr: Qcharging = CFLY × ΔVCFLY;  Qdischarging = idischarge × t = 2 × ILOAD(MAX) × (T / 2)

where.ΔVCFLY: voltage change on the flying capacitor over a cycle
where.T: switching period; each half lasts T / 2

equations.note: Setting the two charges equal gives the minimum flying capacitor.

equations.name: Minimum flying capacitor
equations.note: For 140 mA at 1.5 MHz with a 100 mV allowed change, CFLY comes to 1 μF minimum.

equations.name: Output ripple voltage
equations.expr: VOUT(RIPPLE) = ILOAD(MAX) / (2 × f × COUT) + 2 × ILOAD(MAX) × ESRCOUT

where.ESRCOUT: equivalent series resistance of the output capacitor

equations.note: COUT is at least 2.2 μF for loop stability; a larger or lower-ESR ceramic part lowers the ripple.

equations.name: Efficiency
equations.expr: Efficiency(%) = PD(out) / PD(in) × 100 = (VOUT × IOUT) / (VIN × IIN) × 100, with IIN = 2 × IOUT + IQ

operation.text: A regulated doubler: a 50% duty clock alternates two switch pairs while the control loop holds the flying capacitor at 2.5 V and sets the drop across Q1 and Q2. In the first half-cycle Q2 and Q3 conduct and CF charges to 2.5 V; in the second Q1 and Q4 conduct and CF, stacked on the input, discharges into the output. Output feedback through an internally compensated voltage loop sets VOUT to 5 V, and regulation holds with VIN above 5 V.

Blocks: thermal shutdown and UVLO, a bias circuit, enable logic, a 1.5 MHz oscillator, control, current limit with soft start, regulation of the phase-1 and phase-2 switches, an error amplifier comparing the R1/R2 divided output with VREF, and a skip comparator.
ENA high runs the converter. ENA low puts it in shutdown: the output is cut off from the input and the supply current falls to 10 μA at most.

With a voltage forced onto VOUT the part draws little current back from it, so a connected HDMI or USB OTG device is not drained. Measured with VIN at 3.6 V and EN low, the reverse current stays under about 3.2 μA up to a 5.5 V pre-bias; with VIN open or shorted it stays near zero for either EN state. With VIN at 3.6 V and EN high it is near zero until the pre-bias passes about 5.2 V, then about 14 μA to 15 μA.
Below the UVLO threshold the converter switches off; it restarts once the input climbs back above it, as long as ENA is high.

The output is switched off at a junction temperature near 160°C and turned back on once it cools to about 140°C. Cycling in and out of thermal shutdown over long periods can wear the part. A current limit protects the part and the load as well.
Inrush is held down at enable by a built-in soft start: 150 μs typical from the enable edge to 90% of the output.

When the output reaches 5 V + 0.1 V with the load under about 8 mA, the part stops its oscillator and cuts the output stage's pre-bias, cutting supply current to 90 μA typical. It switches again whenever the output falls below 5 V + 0.1 V, pumping it back up to that level. If the output drops below 5 V the part goes back to normal PWM operation with the oscillator and the output stage at full pre-bias. The skip voltage and current thresholds move with input voltage and load.

A current mirror ties the pass-device current IP to the output current and clamps its maximum at IR3 × k × n, keeping the current limit at 500 mA or less, the limit the HDMI specification requires. With VOUT pulled to ground, the protection senses the low output voltage and pulls Vbias down, folding the output current back to about 80 mA typical. During soft start, from t1 to t2, the available output current climbs from 50 mA minimum to IOUT_MAX while VOUT ramps up to 5.0 V; when VOUT is then shorted to GND the output current drops to the short-circuit level.

USB OTG needs a 5 V rail delivering up to 140 mA, and HDMI a 5 V rail sourcing 55 mA or more; the part can supply either from a battery. It can also drive several white LEDs in parallel through ballast resistors for a small LCD backlight. Other named uses: portable communication devices, PCMCIA cards, mobile phones and handheld meters.

Use a surface-mount ceramic output capacitor for the lowest ripple: tantalum parts have higher ESR, and leaded parts add package inductance, both raising ripple. Ceramic input and flying capacitors give the best results at low input voltage and heavy load. COUT is at least 2.2 μF for stability, CFLY at least 1 μF for 140 mA at 1.5 MHz with 100 mV droop. Only three external capacitors are needed.

Efficiency depends on the output voltage, the input voltage and the load. With the input current about twice the output current, efficiency is near VOUT / (2 × VIN), so it is highest at low input voltage: from 50 mA to 150 mA about 83% to 88% at the bottom of the input range, falling to about 45% at 5.5 V; at 10 mA about 73% falling to about 40%.
Any input source will do as long as its current rating covers what the chip draws at the chosen input voltage and load; the input current is about twice the output current.

VIN, VOUT and GND carry large transient currents. Place all three capacitors right at the chip with short, direct traces to keep input and output ripple down. The exposed thermal pad is soldered down; it carries heat and holds the package. Vias in the pad are optional.
